summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would remove annual expiry requirements for Medicare services tables and repeal outdated administrative provisions from the Health Insurance Act 1973 governing Medicare administration.
Medical, diagnostic imaging and pathology tables would no longer need annual remaking, and obsolete committee references, optometrist undertakings and benefit calculation provisions would be removed.
The changes would concern government administration, while existing patient and health professional arrangements and parliamentary scrutiny of changes to the tables would continue.
changes: References to the inactive Medical Benefits Advisory Committee would be repealed.
The requirement for optometrists to enter an undertaking with the minister would be removed.
An obsolete Medicare compensation recovery provision would be repealed.
A redundant anaesthesia benefit calculation would be removed.
summary.affected: Optometrists providing services funded through Medicare would be affected.

speeches.speaker: Chris Bowen
speeches.brief: The Health Insurance Amendment (Administration) Bill 2020 removes the annual requirement to remake the Medicare Benefits Schedule as a redundant process. The opposition will support the bill but criticises it as minor administrative tinkering, noting record-high out-of-pocket costs and waiting lists, and no reform on private health insurance or broader health system issues.

speeches.speaker: Katrina Allen
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that Australia's healthcare system does not require major reform, citing the country's strong COVID-19 response and record bulk-billing rates, and announced the Health Insurance Amendment (Administration) Bill 2020, which removes the annual sunset period for Medical Benefits Schedule regulations to reduce administrative work and ensure patient entitlements.

speeches.speaker: Luke Howarth
speeches.brief: Supported the Health Insurance Amendment (Administration) Bill 2020, noting the government invested about $24 billion in health last year, and explained the bill removes the annual sunset requirement for Medicare Benefits Schedule regulations to reduce administrative risk, while updating on a federally funded MRI machine for Redcliffe Hospital announced over two years ago.
